body:
OBSERVED 2026-08-29. Of the last 20 `Test Suite` runs on `main`:

| conclusion | count | jobs dispatched |
|---|---|---|
| cancelled | **16** | **0** — every one |
| success | 4 | 6 |

Every cancelled run scheduled **zero jobs**. They were not slow, not starved and not wedged: they
were cancelled by the next push before GitHub allocated them a runner.

`.github/workflows/tests.yml` sets

    concurrency:
      group: ${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }}
      cancel-in-progress: true

That is exactly right for a PR branch, where only the latest head matters. On `main` it means each
push cancels the previous commit's verification, and under a high merge rate — this repo runs ~10
concurrent sessions merging — a run rarely survives the ~2-4 minutes before a runner picks it up.
The result is that **the only main commit that gets tested is the last one before a quiet period.**

Nothing surfaces this. A cancelled run is not a red run: no alert fires, `auto-revert` skips, and
anything asking "is main green?" sees the last *successful* run, which may be several commits old.
Meanwhile `Build & Push - Dev` for those same commits completes and publishes — F-7786b7 (":dev
publishes from commits whose Test Suite never passed") observed live, and now with a mechanism.

⚠️ RETRACTION — an earlier version of this finding said main's runs were "wedged, never
dispatched", called it "not a FIFO queue", and listed six rejected hypotheses. The observation was
right; the conclusion was wrong, and the reasoning that produced it is worth recording:

- "15 runs created after main's had already completed while main's had zero jobs" was TRUE, and I
  read it as main being starved. Those were **branch** runs, which have their own per-ref
  concurrency groups and so were never competing with main's.
- `gh run rerun` refusing with "already running" looked like a wedge; it is what GitHub says about
  a run that is pending.
- Cancelling the pending run and dispatching a fresh one "reproduced" the symptom — but my
  dispatched run was then itself cancelled by the #1971 merge push. I had built the very thing I
  was measuring.
- Hypothesis 2 (concurrency-group deadlock) was rejected because "the group was freed and the
  successor still did not dispatch". The successor was cancelled too. That rejection was wrong, and
  the truth is adjacent to it: not a deadlock, but the concurrency policy nonetheless.

The tell I missed: I read `status` and job counts, never `conclusion`. Sixteen `cancelled` rows
were sitting in the same API response the whole time.

FIX SHAPE, cheapest first:
1. Drop `cancel-in-progress` for `main` (keep it for `pull_request`) — a per-ref conditional, so
   every commit that lands gets verified even if runs queue up behind each other.
2. Or accept the trade and make it visible: fail loudly, or record which commits were never tested,
   so "main is green" cannot silently mean "some ancestor of main was green".
3. Regardless: anything gating on main's CI should treat `cancelled` as *unknown*, never as pass.

COUNTER-EVIDENCE, so nobody acts on this in the wrong direction: the tree is fine. `origin/main`
was verified directly in a detached worktree (7506 passed, 106 skipped, 0 failed, SHA identical
before and after), and run `33234685635` later went green in CI across all six jobs including E2E
and Docker integration. This is a verification-coverage problem, not a broken main.
title: cancel-in-progress on main discards ~80% of Test Suite runs before they dispatch, so most commits land unverified
